One ongoing frustration is the lack of effort I see being put towards near-term, achievable crash projects to do good with AI at a national scale, whether those efforts are by the AI labs or by policymakers & NGOs.

Some obvious ideas to explore suggested by the data we have so far: universal tutoring to support classroom learning, second opinions on healthcare, financial literacy/scam avoidance, and making government services easy to access.

These are hard problems, and I know because over the past 20 years I have worked extensively on building tutoring and financial literacy programs, which were always limited by existing technology. Now, real gains are likely achievable with AI, which should be a big deal. Yes, you would want to do careful design and studies before rolling things out. And yes, those efforts might fail. But, if done right, national programs could lead to big gains in public good for seemingly intractable problems. And they don't require AIs beyond current models to pull off.

blogs.content:
(Photo by Jon Cherry/Getty Images)

 Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery!

 As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone . Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings .

 On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week.

 AI on the Ballot. This week’s elections delivered Democrats the largest Congressional majority either party has enjoyed in 36 years, and coupled with a variety of similar results at the state level (particularly in Texas), not to mention plenty of data center opposition among Republicans, the future of the AI buildout is now fraught with more regulatory uncertainty than ever. I wrote about X, 2024 symmetry, and the more political aspects of the election for Sharp Text , while Ben’s Article on Wednesday built on his data center warnings from April and provided 10 takes on the post-midterms landscape for tech companies. — Andrew Sharp

 A Google State of the Union. Last week Google reported earnings and saw growth in search revenue slow for the first time in five quarters. Given the appearance of mortality in what might be the greatest business in the history of digital commerce, investors were predictably spooked. However, I think the company deserves time to see if AI Mode ends up like Stories and Reels did for Facebook: if anyone can monetize AI with ads, it’s going to be Google. On Sharp Tech , we also got into why Google’s AI bet is about more than AI Mode, and why I find myself impressed by Google’s fortitude, even if the rest of the Internet is a casualty. — Ben Thompson

 And What About China? Elections have consequences, as they say, so what might a Democratic Congressional majority mean for the next two years of U.S.-China relations? We tried to answer that question on Sharp China this week , including predicting factional foreign policy fights between the left and center-left, highlighting the profound unknowns concerning President Trump’s posture after this week’s defeat, and offering one safe bet in the new environment: life is about to get a lot more complicated for Jensen Huang in Washington. — AS

---

 Presented by

 I spend a lot of time trying to figure out what is happening to businesses on the internet. What I often find I’m missing is a view across the economy itself. With more than 1.7% of global GDP running on Stripe, working with them means I can bring some of what they’re seeing to Stratechery. They are, in a sense, a barometer of the economy.

 Take the “SaaSpocalypse”. Earlier this year, nearly a trillion dollars in enterprise software value disappeared amid fears of AI eating its lunch. Stock prices only tell us what investors think will happen, and not necessarily what is happening. In this case, Stripe recently built a SaaS Index using payments data from 72,000 non-AI SaaS businesses. Looking at their actual performance, we can see that while SaaS stocks were selling off, revenue growth was actually accelerating.

Year-over-year growth is now over 30%, with some of the fastest growth coming from the youngest SaaS companies. I suspect there are a lot more interesting things hiding in Stripe’s data, and I’m excited about having an excuse to go look for them.

---

 Stratechery Articles and Updates

 Google Earnings, Facebook Déjà Vu, The Agent Play — Google’s earnings miss looks a lot like Facebook’s, and that’s a credit to Google. The company is being more aggressive than they get credit for.

 Apple Earnings, Memory Problems, The Hardware Company Regression — Apple’s earnings suggest that the company’s hardware business is doing better than ever, even in the face of memory challenges. Does the software story help or hurt?

 AI on the Ballot — Data Centers were on the ballot, and they lost in a major way; what does it mean if American opposition to building is permanent?

 An Interview With Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi About Accounting and AI — An interview with Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi about the working for one of tech’s oldest software companies, and how Intuit is leaning into the AI paradigm shift.

 Sharp Text by Andrew Sharp

 X Marks the Rot — Republicans colonized Twitter and then cannibalized their support with two years of memes, corruption and excess.

 Dithering with Ben Thompson and Daring Fireball’s John Gruber

 DoorDash and Google

 The MacBook Pro (with touch)

 Asianometry with Jon Yu

 The Rise of GLM and China’s Zhipu AI

 Sharp China with Andrew Sharp and Sinocism’s Bill Bishop

 Parsing the Fifth Plenum; US-China After the Midterms; New Scrutiny for Nvidia?; Cybersecurity and Espionage

 Greatest of All Talk

 The Rapture and the Wild West, Luka Doncic on Praise Probation, AJ Dybantsa Saves the Wizards

 Sharp Tech with Andrew Sharp and Ben Thompson

 Subscriber Mail: Apple Past and Present, Omarchy, Instacart, and Baseball

 America Votes Against Data Centers, Implications for Big Tech and Beyond, Were Google Bears Right All Along?

 This week’s Stratechery video is on The End of the Internet .

blogs.content:
The products aren't good enough to sell people on the costs.

 You cannot tell people that you have to listen to the whine of a data center in their backyard for AI overviews and some of the most hilarious deep fake slop in history.

 It's not worth it. It just isn't worth it to anyone. And agents aren't real and they might not be being used the way that anyone wants them to yet. All these companies are spending more than they're making on these products. Refrigerators holding blood storage in Europe are being hacked.

 The costs are too high. The benefits are not real. And if you connect that to corruption, you're like, in order to impose these costs on me, these CEOs are in the White House shaking Trump's hand, renaming it to the Gulf of America, paying for this ballroom that we don't want. It's obvious crypto-corruption, and it's still slop.

 The AI industry will not get out of it until they make better products . Until everyone can see without needing to be convinced, without needing an ad campaign, without any of this stuff that just using these products makes your life better.

 — Nilay Patel , The Vergecast: Big Tech lost big in the 2026 election

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 4,687 new readers. Anthropic has made “pacing the frontier” part of its pitch, holding back on what it hands the public. Inside the lab, the pace appears to be a different story.
 After 11 weeks inside the lab’s data, METR estimates Anthropic’s progress has roughly doubled, with its own AI driving most of the jump and no clear bottlenecks to slow it down. When the public gets to see the models behind it is another question.

---

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 ANTHROPIC
 📈  METR’s inside look at Anthropic’s AI speedup
 Image source: METR

 The Rundown: AI-evaluation nonprofit METR just published a new report on its findings from 11 weeks of inside access to Anthropic’s internal data and interviews with staff, concluding the company’s AI progress is likely running about 2x as fast as before, mostly due to its own AI — though Anthropic redacted most of the strongest evidence.
 The details:
 METR’s estimated range of speedup over Anthropic’s 2024–25 pace runs from 1.3 to 3x, with METR crediting AI for around 80% of the company’s faster progress.

 Anthropic co-founder and safety lead Sam McCandlish said the lab’s heavy redactions were to avoid “handing out a roadmap for others to go faster.”

 The report also revealed two internal models ahead of its top-ranked Claude Opus 5.5, including a “Model 4” that cleared 50% on all 15 tested benchmarks.

 Anthropic’s IPO filing defined a danger threshold as “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI,” with Monday’s update saying that point may be close.

 Why it matters: METR’s own Ryan Greenblatt said he was “seriously wrong” after expecting a much slower speedup this year. AI helping build better AI is the loop every lab is chasing and every safety plan worries about, and it already seems to be running inside Anthropic. With METR spotting no clear bottlenecks, that loop may only get faster.

 TOGETHER WITH GRANOLA
 ⌨️  Your favorite notetaker now does the typing too

 The Rundown: Granola, the AI notepad for people with back-to-back meetings, just launched Voice Typing. Hold Fn and talk, and clean text appears in any app, whether you’re replying to an email or writing a prompt.
 With Voice Typing, you can:
 Speak naturally and get clean text in Gmail, Slack, or Docs

 Dictate in any app, outside Granola

 Use it now on Mac and Windows, iOS and Android coming soon

 Get your first month free with code THERUNDOWN .

 ROWAN’S CORNER
 3️⃣ The ‘Three Times’ rule
 Image source: The Rundown @ Google I/O

 Rowan: I have a rule before I’m allowed to automate anything: I have to do it manually at least three times first.
 Every automation I’ve shared here has followed it. I ran my Friday “factory inspections” by hand for months before handing them to an agent . I sorted my contacts and wrote my own follow-ups before my agents took those over . The manual reps were the training data for my own judgment.
 When you do a task yourself a few times, you learn what good looks like, which steps actually matter, and where things tend to go wrong (that’s what also lets you check an agent’s work later instead of blindly trusting it).
 It also fixes the most common mistake I see when people start building with AI, which is going into the tools looking for problems to solve. Flip it. Find the real problems in your life and work first, do them manually three times, then (and only then) automate them. The time you free up will surface the next problem, and then you repeat.
 That loop is how real AI productivity happens. It’s never one tool automating everything at once; it’s an iterative process that stacks, and six months in you’re a different operator.
 So before you build the agent, do the task yourself on Monday, again on Wednesday, and again on Friday. Then automate the version you actually understand.

 AI TRAINING
 💼  Use AI to find a job and prepare to get hired

 The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll use AI to find real job openings, compare them with your experience, tailor your resume, and practice for an interview. One fictional applicant carries through the full process, so you can follow along before using your own details.
 Step-by-step:
 Choose one target job title, two related titles, and your limits for location, work setup, salary, and experience.

 Ask ChatGPT to find five current openings. Check each role on the employer’s own careers page before adding it to your list.

 Compare one verified job description with a redacted copy of your resume. Ask AI to show strong matches, partial matches, and missing requirements.

 Tailor the resume and write a short cover letter using only facts you can support. Review every new claim before saving or applying.

 Practice eight interview questions, one at a time, then add the application and next follow-up date to your tracker.

 Pro tip: Ask AI to show the evidence behind every resume change. A keyword is useful only when it describes work you’ve actually done.

 The Rundown: Agentic AI investment is up 31.8%, but only 11% of organizations turn that into measurable business value. The 2027 CIO Agenda identifies four critical disconnects and what leading organizations do to bridge the gap to value.

 Why ambition outpaces budgets

 OPENAI
 🖼️ OpenAI’s Images 2.6 adds GIFs to ChatGPT
 Image source: OpenAI

 The Rundown: OpenAI just released Images 2.6, an upgraded, faster image model family rolling out across its ChatGPT and Codex platforms with new built-in GIF capabilities that can animate a typed idea, photo, or sketch.
 The details:
 OAI already held the top spot across image benchmarks with its previous models, and 2.6 edges just past its predecessor for No. 1 on Design Arena .

 Two versions are available for developers via API, with Sunburst for higher-quality work and Flare for lighter, faster jobs.

 2.6 is the first OpenAI image model to add motion, able to convert existing images or ideas into moving GIFs or create entirely new animations from scratch.

 Users can change a GIF’s speed or rework single frames, with the company saying the model also generates images 50% faster than previous versions.

 Why it matters: Fun? Yes. The Astra 6.2 upgrade everyone wanted? No. OpenAI still leads in image generation, but with Anthropic topping the main AI leaderboards for months, anything short of the next major model release (widely expected this week) is an appetizer.

blogs.description: The cost of breaking into a corporate network with AI has fallen 99% in five months, & corporate security budgets are racing to catch up. G…
blogs.content:
The cost of breaking into a corporate network with AI has fallen 99% in five months, & corporate security budgets are racing to catch up.

 Goldman executives have discussed how the firm could soon be on track to spend as much or more on AI for security than it spends on AI coding tools. 1 , 2

 Security has been a collection of layers of defense, each an insurance policy against a particular kind of attack. 1 As autonomous AI threats become the predominant risk, both attackers & defenders are competing on how much AI compute they can deploy.

 An attacker’s math is an expected-value calculation on compute. Spend $1m of AI tokens trying to break into a bank with a 1% chance at a $1b payout, & the expected value is $10m : a $9m expected profit. Spend that same compute on a 5% chance at a $500k payout, & the expected return is $25k : a $975k loss. Because cheap defensive filters block low-effort noise, rational attackers stop spraying small targets & concentrate their tokens on the largest balance sheets.

 Defenders face a harder equation : how much defensive AI it takes to neutralize each dollar of offensive AI.

 In April, Anthropic & OpenAI tested whether Claude Mythos Preview & GPT-5.5 could break into a simulated British corporate network : a 32-step hack across 20 servers that takes a human expert 20 hours. 3 , 4 Both models took over the network without human help, & the Bank for International Settlements priced the break-in at $5k to $10k. 3

 Five months later, the price of that same break-in has fallen 99%. Claude Mythos 5 dropped the cost to $770 in June, Claude Opus 5 to $385 in July, & Zhipu’s open-weight GLM-5.3 matches Mythos’s exploit rate for $90 : one-sixtieth of April’s frontier cost. 5

 In the security operations center, AI agents relieve overwhelmed human teams who face more than 4,400 alerts a day & historically lacked the hours to examine two-thirds of them : autonomous investigations compress a 70-minute manual review into minutes for about $2 of compute per alert, freeing analysts to focus on real intrusions. 6

 Yet the cost ratio still starts tilted toward the attacker, because the SOC must inspect every alert, every hour. 3 , 7

 Three multipliers compound that defensive compute requirement :

 First, speed : Glean CISO Sunil Agrawal notes that AI compresses intrusion response from months to minutes, while CrowdStrike records average breakout times of 29 minutes & a fastest of 27 seconds. 8 , 9

 Second, scale : in the July 2026 intrusion at Hugging Face, a swarm of 700 AI agents coordinated across four & a half days, exchanging 70,000 messages & executing 17,600 actions until they harvested 136 production keys, & Cogent Research finds 76% of new monthly enterprise attack paths (up 386% year over year) are viable only for parallel AI swarms. 10

 Third, breadth : non-human identities already outnumber employees 82 to 1, & as enterprise agent fleets scale to 100x headcount, every new agent expands the surface area to defend. 11 , 12

 The CISO’s job is no longer stacking per-seat insurance policies. It is maximizing the efficiency & effectiveness of the security stack : buying enough compute, & converting it into enough defensive tokens, to drive the attacker’s expected value below zero.

---

blogs.title: The components of agent memory
blogs.description: Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood backward, but it must be lived forward. We’ve encountered a similar bind when…
blogs.content:
Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood backward , but it must be lived forward . We’ve encountered a similar bind when designing memory for AI agents.
 As humans, we encode memory constantly as we go about our lives. The hippocampus plays a central role in this, capturing experiences in the moment so that memories form quickly and are immediately available. But only some experiences are consolidated into long-term knowledge.
 Much of that consolidation appears to happen when our brains are offline. As we sleep, and during quiet rest , the hippocampus replays our recent experiences. This is thought to gradually distill those experiences and integrate them into the neocortex—the part of our brains that stores most of what we think of as knowledge.
 Agent memory can use a similar division of labor. Agents capture much of their work in logs or transcripts. Researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley proposed sleep-time compute as a way for models to use idle time between interactions to reorganize their existing context. The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often called dreaming (Figure 1).
 We’ve found that dreaming has been a useful tool for helping us give Claude effective memory. In this post, we share how we’ve come to think about agent memory and walk through several evaluations we’ve used to explore agent memory, including the use of dreaming, and what each component contributes to memory organization.
 Claude can use dreaming to organize memory. This can correct mistakes, create notes, build new memory representations, or shape what’s preemptively loaded into future sessions.

 Memory notes
 By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later. It excludes other ways models can learn or manage context, such as changes to their weights (the internal parameters set during training), in-context learning (knowledge gained within a single conversation), and compaction (summaries written by Claude that replace its older turns so it can continue working in a new context window).
 In the human brain, chemical signals released before, during, or after an experience can mark a memory as important. Marked memories tend to be replayed more often than unmarked ones during offline periods. This process, called replay , helps stabilize and integrate them into long-term memory.
 Similarly, Claude can tag salient events in a session log as they happen, so they’re easier to find later, or it can write them to a memory store, such as a folder of memory notes (Figure 2). But how can Claude tell what’s salient in the moment, before it knows what’s coming next?
 Claude can write notes to memory.

 Memory can be a prediction about what the future will need
 Memory is, occasionally, a prediction. By writing down a rule, an agent predicts that the pattern it’s describing will be relevant again. For instance, writing down a verified fact is a prediction that an agent in a future session will want to rely on that fact without double-checking it. Over time, Claude has become much better at making these kinds of predictions.
 Consider a task from Continual Learning Bench (CL-Bench) 1.0 , a benchmark that measures an agent’s ability to use memory in order to tackle long-horizon tasks. One particular task asks Claude to answer a series of questions by looking up information in a database. After Claude gives an answer, it’s told the correct solution and can write a memory to help answer future questions.
 Memory can support a learning loop here. If Claude gets a question wrong, it can record the failure, come up with theories about what went wrong, test those theories, and turn what it finds into a rule about how to answer in the future.
 We ran the CL-Bench 1.0 task using Claude Managed Agents . Claude started each question in a fresh session, with one exception: it could retrieve files from a memory directory that persisted from one session to the next.
 Different models achieved different levels of success at creating their own learning loops. Claude Sonnet 4.6 got as far as generating theories about why an answer was wrong. Its memory directory contained a scattering of files, each listing several untested guesses.
 CL-Bench database task, comparing memory with a stateless baseline across models.

 Claude Opus 4.7 consolidated its notes into a single reference document and began marking which facts it had checked and which were still unconfirmed. Claude Sonnet 5 marked each answer as confirmed after the grader had checked it, and wrote a correction when it had answered wrong.
 Claude Opus 5 was the first of these models to close the loop. Most of its entries included a rule (and also how it knew the rule was true), answers to earlier questions, and clear warnings about traps it had discovered along the way (Figure 3).
 Like Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 both closed the loop, using memory to capture validated rules about how to best answer future questions. With memory, both scored about the same as Opus 5, though their baseline performance without memory was slightly higher.
 Claude has learned to judge salience
 We also evaluated Claude’s ability to play Pokémon Red , a game that challenges Claude to navigate complex long-horizon tasks, as a test of Claude’s judgment about what to save to memory. At the start of each run, we gave each model a folder of memory files that it could read from and write to while it played (Figure 4).
 We compared the memory folders from one run each of Claude Sonnet 3.7 and Claude Fable 5, when each was about 10,000 steps into the game. A key difference we noticed was what each model thought was worth remembering. Sonnet 3.7 assumed everything might matter and wrote to memory indiscriminately. Its memory folder contained an archive of encounters, often with a separate file for each battle it fought, each item it found, and each non-player character it met. Ultimately, Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files across 225 folders and earned one badge (badges mark a player’s progress through the game).
 Fable 5, by comparison, wrote nine files in two folders, plus a single top-level file called global.md , and earned four badges.
 Claude’s memory directories for Sonnet 3.7 versus Fable 5 while playing Pokémon.

 Sonnet 3.7’s approach was a problem mainly because the game state of Pokémon changes constantly—Sonnet 3.7’s detailed record was continuously going out of date. As a result, as Claude progressed, it had to spend more time and resources combing through its memories rather than playing the game. Around step 10,000, for example, Sonnet 3.7 started its fourth folder of “master” memory files. Over the next 17 steps, it created six files, deleted nine others, and took no actions in the game itself.
 Fable 5’s approach used memory for things the game didn’t explicitly tell it. Some of the kinds of information Sonnet 3.7 wrote to memory—such as how much money the player has or where the player is on the map—can be read off the screen every turn, so storing it is redundant. By contrast, memory files about strategy, plans, and tested rules exist only if Claude works them out, and they disappear unless Claude writes them down.
 Fable 5 organized its memory accordingly. Its global.md file acted as a dashboard, holding the current goal, a prewritten plan for tackling gyms (the challenges where badges are won), and the model’s own rules for using memory. A locations folder held plans for navigating particular routes, and a gameplay folder held strategies based on what it had learned about how the game works. For example, after seven Poké Balls in a row failed to catch a Magikarp (one of the easiest Pokémon to catch), Claude wrote, “If 3+ balls fail in a row, VARY the timing (insert extra ‘wait’ presses between menu steps) - the catch landed right after doing this.”
 With a much smaller memory folder, Fable 5 progressed much further in the game than Sonnet 3.7. Opus 5.5 took a similar approach: it kept a small folder of memory notes that tracked its current goal and next steps, rewrote them as it played, and beat the game.
 Steering Claude to write memory
 We’ve found that it helps to tell Claude what memory is for, but not how to use it. On CL-Bench, we simply told Claude that a memory folder was available. That general guidance was enough for Opus 4.7 and Opus 5 to use memory effectively, and it gave both a noticeable boost in performance (Figure 3).
 We also tested giving the models specific rules about what they should write to memory, with one rule per test. We compared how much each model gained from memory with each rule against how much it gained without it. When we set a rule to “record only failures,” both Opus 5 and Opus 4.7 lost much of the performance boost that memory gave them (Figure 5, right). For stronger models, giving them freedom to judge salience was more effective than setting fixed rules in advance, and those rules could end up weakening performance.
 Left: Sonnet 4.6 on the CL-Bench database task with and without prompting to guide memory usage. Right: how much each model’s gain from memory changed when it was told to record only failures.

 We also noticed that steering helped older models the most. For instance, Sonnet 4.6 often didn’t read files from its memory directory and failed to test its theories about why an answer was wrong.
 In this case, prompting Claude to read its memory files before answering—and then to explicitly test its theories—nearly doubled its benchmark score (Figure 5, left). Sonnet 5 does this on its own. Without being prompted to, it read its memory before answering 9 out of 10 times. By comparison, Sonnet 4.6 did this less than half of the time.
 With frontier Claude models, we typically give simple guidance to create memory notes when a person asks them to or when something is clearly worth remembering, and we leave that judgment up to Claude.
 Dreaming can correct memory
 Since Claude writes to memory based on what it judges to be salient in-session, a note that’s wrong from the start or that drifts as the environment changes can be read, and trusted, by Claude in a later session.
 Dreaming gives Claude a way to test its notes against the original transcripts (Figure 6). We saw a positive example of this when Claude played Pokémon using Managed Agents with a mounted directory for its memories.
 Dreaming can correct mistakes in memory.

 In one part of the game, the player has to get through Mt. Moon, a cave system with its entrance on the west side of the map and its exit on the east. Near the entrance is a trap: a one-way ledge that drops the player onto the route they came from, with no clear way to climb back up. Claude was using the PokéCenter, a building at the mountain’s entrance, as a landmark, so whether it walked off the ledge depended on which side of the mountain it thought the PokéCenter was on.
 At one point, Claude wrote down (incorrectly) that the PokéCenter was on the east side. When it walked out of the PokéCenter, it announced, “Mt Moon is behind me,” and updated its notes: “Mt Moon DONE.” But Mt. Moon was not behind it. A few actions later, Claude went over the ledge and landed back on the route it had come from (Figure 7). Its navigation tool didn’t show the drop, so Claude concluded, “I overshot far west,” and that it had been on the correct side all along. It hadn’t.
 A corrected memory note changed the outcome in Pokémon. With the uncorrected note, Claude says, “Mt Moon is behind me,” heads for the next city, and ends up back on the route it came from. With the note corrected by dreaming, it says, “Now I need to find the Mt Moon cave entrance to re-enter,” and goes back into the cave.

The best Stratechery content from the week of November 2, 2026, including AI on the ballot, a Google state of the union, and China.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

(Photo by Jon Cherry/Getty Images)
Welcome back to This Week in Stratechery!

As a reminder, each week, every Friday, we’re sending out this overview of content in the Stratechery bundle; highlighted links are free for everyone . Additionally, you have complete control over what we send to you. If you don’t want to receive This Week in Stratechery emails (there is no podcast), please uncheck the box in your delivery settings .

On that note, here were a few of our favorites this week.

AI on the Ballot. This week’s elections delivered Democrats the largest Congressional majority either party has enjoyed in 36 years, and coupled with a variety of similar results at the state level (particularly in Texas), not to mention plenty of data center opposition among Republicans, the future of the AI buildout is now fraught with more regulatory uncertainty than ever. I wrote about X, 2024 symmetry, and the more political aspects of the election for Sharp Text , while Ben’s Article on Wednesday built on his data center warnings from April and provided 10 takes on the post-midterms landscape for tech companies. — Andrew Sharp

A Google State of the Union. Last week Google reported earnings and saw growth in search revenue slow for the first time in five quarters. Given the appearance of mortality in what might be the greatest business in the history of digital commerce, investors were predictably spooked. However, I think the company deserves time to see if AI Mode ends up like Stories and Reels did for Facebook: if anyone can monetize AI with ads, it’s going to be Google. On Sharp Tech , we also got into why Google’s AI bet is about more than AI Mode, and why I find myself impressed by Google’s fortitude, even if the rest of the Internet is a casualty. — Ben Thompson

And What About China? Elections have consequences, as they say, so what might a Democratic Congressional majority mean for the next two years of U.S.-China relations? We tried to answer that question on Sharp China this week , including predicting factional foreign policy fights between the left and center-left, highlighting the profound unknowns concerning President Trump’s posture after this week’s defeat, and offering one safe bet in the new environment: life is about to get a lot more complicated for Jensen Huang in Washington. — AS

---

Presented by

I spend a lot of time trying to figure out what is happening to businesses on the internet. What I often find I’m missing is a view across the economy itself. With more than 1.7% of global GDP running on Stripe, working with them means I can bring some of what they’re seeing to Stratechery. They are, in a sense, a barometer of the economy.

Take the “SaaSpocalypse”. Earlier this year, nearly a trillion dollars in enterprise software value disappeared amid fears of AI eating its lunch. Stock prices only tell us what investors think will happen, and not necessarily what is happening. In this case, Stripe recently built a SaaS Index using payments data from 72,000 non-AI SaaS businesses. Looking at their actual performance, we can see that while SaaS stocks were selling off, revenue growth was actually accelerating.

Year-over-year growth is now over 30%, with some of the fastest growth coming from the youngest SaaS companies. I suspect there are a lot more interesting things hiding in Stripe’s data, and I’m excited about having an excuse to go look for them.
